meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Some cause happiness wherever they go; others whenever they go'?
meta.ogDescription: Wilde died in 1900. The gag is documented from May 1908 as anonymous magazine filler and was only pinned on Wilde in 1955.

answer.label: Not Oscar Wilde — an anonymous 1908 magazine joke
answer.authorDates: First documented May 1908 · creator never named
answer.sourceLine: The earliest instance located by Quote Investigator ↗ is an unsigned filler item in Success Magazine in May 1908, headed “Others Whenever” — no creator was named. The gag circulated anonymously for decades; the first known book to hand it to Oscar Wilde is Herbert V. Prochnow’s Speaker’s Handbook of Epigrams and Witticisms in 1955, more than half a century after Wilde’s death in 1900.

docMeta.dd: A Little Book of Aphorisms (1947), printed as ANON.

source.excerpt: Some agents create happiness wherever they go; others whenever they go.
trail: May 1908 — the earliest instance located by Quote Investigator ↗ is a short unsigned item in Success Magazine headed “Others Whenever,” reading “Some people make happiness wherever they go.” The punchline sat in the headline, and no author was credited.
13 May 1908 — The Insurance Press ran the earliest version QI documents ↗ with both halves in a single sentence: “Some agents create happiness wherever they go; others whenever they go.”

1934 – 1947 — humorist Olin Miller used the gag in his “Sunland Shorts” column in The Miami News on 15 October 1934, but QI notes ↗ it was already in circulation. The exact wording quoted today appears in Frederick B. Wilcox’s A Little Book of Aphorisms (Charles Scribner’s Sons, 1947), labelled ANON.

1955 — the earliest attribution to Wilde is Herbert V. Prochnow’s Speaker’s Handbook of Epigrams and Witticisms, whose 1955 Harper first edition ↗ is catalogued at Open Library; Wikiquote ↗ files the line under “Disputed” and records the same 1955 starting point.
source.excerptNote: This is the earliest single-line version documented by Quote Investigator that carries both halves of the joke — written for an insurance trade readership, hence “agents.” The general wording familiar today is not recorded until Frederick B. Wilcox’s 1947 collection, where it is printed as anonymous.

source.rightsNote: The saying is anonymous. Its earliest documented forms appeared in American magazines in May 1908, but the precise wording quoted today is first recorded in a 1947 collection, A Little Book of Aphorisms, where it is printed unattributed as ANON. Because no author and no single originating publication can be tied to this exact sentence, Quotle asserts no copyright status for it.

author.name: Anonymous
author.heading: Who actually wrote it
author.metaLine: First documented May 1908 · United States · unsigned magazine filler
author.bio: No individual has ever been credibly identified as the author of this joke. It surfaces in May 1908 as an unsigned filler item in Success Magazine, and within the same month appears in the Harrisburg Star-Independent, the St. Joseph Daily Press and the New York trade paper The Insurance Press — the classic signature of an unattributed gag travelling the reprint circuit. Later figures associated with it, including the humorist Olin Miller in 1934, were repeating a line that was already in wide circulation.

misattribution.heading: Why Wilde gets the credit
misattribution.intro: Oscar Wilde is one of the internet’s great quote magnets: a line only has to be short and clever to end up under his name. This one has a documented origin that has nothing to do with him, and a documented moment where the mix-up begins.

items.why: Wilde died in 1900; the joke is not documented until 1908. Quote Investigator ↗ states it has found “no substantive evidence” that Wilde employed the saying, and Wikiquote ↗ lists it under “Disputed,” noting no source in Wilde’s writings has been found.

In Frederick B. Wilcox’s A Little Book of Aphorisms (1947), the anonymous line is printed immediately after a genuine Wilde quotation. QI ↗ points to “the misreading of neighboring quotations” as a major engine of misattribution and suggests inattentive readers of that book decided the second statement was Wilde’s.

items.scope: The book that printed it as Wilde’s
items.who: Herbert V. Prochnow, Speaker’s Handbook of Epigrams and Witticisms (1955)
items.why: This Harper volume is the earliest source in which the joke is ascribed to Wilde, per Quote Investigator ↗; a catalogue record ↗ confirms the 1955 first edition. Handbooks like it were mined by later quotation compilers, which is how a stray credit becomes permanent.

items.scope: The other name in the file
items.why: The humorist ran the joke in The Miami News on 15 October 1934, and some sources credit him. QI ↗ is explicit that the gag was already in circulation by then.
A widely shared alternative ends “whenever they leave.” QI ↗ records that form in the Chicago Daily Tribune in 1956 — later than the “whenever they go” versions, and equally anonymous.

misattribution.truthLine: It is an anonymous American magazine joke, first documented in May 1908, that drifted onto Oscar Wilde’s name in the mid-twentieth century — see Quote Investigator’s full citation trail ↗.

context.heading: A joke built for filler columns
lead: The line began life as newspaper and magazine filler — the one-sentence gags that editors dropped in to close out a column. That is exactly why no author’s name is attached: filler was routinely reprinted, reworded and re-headlined without credit. In May 1908 Success Magazine ran it with the punchline hidden in the headline, “Others Whenever,” and within weeks Pennsylvania and Michigan papers had picked it up, according to the citation trail assembled by Quote Investigator ↗.

Its shape is what keeps it alive: a compliment that turns into an insult on the last word. That structure also makes it feel Wildean, which is probably why the 1955 credit stuck so hard. But feeling like Wilde is not evidence of Wilde — and the documented record runs from an unsigned 1908 filler item through an anonymous 1947 aphorism collection before his name ever appears.
detailsBody: Tracking the exact wording matters here. The 1908 versions read “Some people make happiness wherever they go” and “Some agents create happiness wherever they go; others whenever they go.” Olin Miller’s 1934 column has “There are some who cause happiness wherever they go, others whenever they go.” The tidy modern form — “Some cause happiness wherever they go; others whenever they go” — is first recorded in 1947, and it is printed there as anonymous.

No edition of Wilde’s plays, essays, letters or poems has ever been shown to contain the line. His complete works are freely readable at Project Gutenberg ↗, and the absence is not for want of searching: this is one of the most-checked Wilde attributions on the internet.
context.pull: The punchline was in the headline: “Others Whenever.”
